deep.reconstruction:
The page is almost entirely drawings, with a few pencil abbreviations. It belongs to Grothendieck's 1983-84 notes on 'systèmes de pseudo-droites', which concern topological and combinatorial arrangements of pseudolines in the disc or projective plane. The previous and next pages show pseudoline arrangements in discs, so the reading below fits that context; most of it is interpretation of drawings, not something the page states.

(1) Left drawing (felt pens). A disc, read as a hemisphere or affine chart of the projective plane, is cut into cells by a brown-purple graph.
- The cells are a central, roughly pentagonal cell, a ring of about five larger cells around it, and boundary cells meeting the circle.
- Blue: a dual graph. It has one vertex in each cell, one edge crossing each brown edge, and edges running out of the disc to 'infinity'.
- Green: cone or star structures. The central cell is coned from a green centre point with spokes to its vertices. The boundary cells are coned from green points on the boundary circle.
- Orange: rounded curves running just inside the central cell and arcs around the boundary points. They look like boundaries of regular or star neighbourhoods, or a 'thickened' version of the cell structure.
- Overall this looks like the CW decomposition from an arrangement, together with its dual and a subdivision or star-neighbourhood structure. Such structure is relevant to the topological or isotopy classification of arrangements (stratifications, dual complexes, links of cells).

(2) Dashed lines. Short dashed lines run from the right edge of the disc toward the two wave diagrams. This suggests the wave diagrams 'unroll' the boundary region (the neighbourhood of the line at infinity, or of the equator) along a horizontal line.
- Orange: X-shaped crossings strung along the line, i.e. pairs of curves crossing near the line.
- Green: curves oscillating above and below the line. They plausibly trace the zig-zag profile of cells adjacent to the boundary.
- The green curve crosses the horizontal line several times, so it is not a pseudoline relative to that line. It reads as a cell-boundary profile, not a member of the arrangement.

(3) Pencil, top right. A circle with a hatched polygonal cell structure on part of it, and small Λ-triangles sitting on the lower boundary. These are cells (triangles) adjacent to the boundary circle.

(4) Pencil, middle. A horizontal baseline carries a row of small triangles: Δ above the line, ∇ below, some hatched. Each triangle has a two-line abbreviation, roughly 'p.a.h. / s.g.g.', 'p.s.a / m.s.g', with some crossed out, and one line reads 'i.g.a.i. out'.
- This looks like a case-by-case classification of triangular cells adjacent to a distinguished line (the line at infinity or a chosen pseudoline), by side and orientation.
- Possible meanings of the abbreviations include up/down, left/right and sense of rotation. The text is too illegible to decode reliably.
- Triangles adjacent to a line are the classical objects in Levi's theorem and its refinements (every line in a simple projective arrangement borders at least three triangles; there are at least n triangles overall). They are also the basis of triangle-flip moves (Ringel), which act as the elementary isotopies or mutations between arrangements.

In modern terms, the page studies the local combinatorics of the cell complex of a pseudoline arrangement near a line or the boundary, the dual graph, and the triangles adjacent to that line. This is groundwork for describing elementary moves or a normal form, but nothing is stated or proved.
errors: No mathematical claims are written, so nothing can be checked as true or false.

The green 'wave' curves cross the horizontal reference line repeatedly, so they cannot be pseudolines of the same arrangement as that line. They must be auxiliary curves, e.g. cell-boundary profiles; the drawing is consistent with that reading.
The meaning of the abbreviations is undetermined, so any classification they encode cannot be verified.

ideas.what: Cell decomposition of the disc/projective plane by a pseudoline-type arrangement, drawn with its dual graph (blue), including edges to the line at infinity.
ideas.modern_name: Cell complex of an arrangement and its dual graph (tope graph / zonotopal tiling dual)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926), Grünbaum (1972); for the oriented-matroid view Folkman–Lawrence (1978), Edelman, Björner–Las Vergnas–Sturmfels–White–Ziegler
ideas.where_published: Not in published texts; the pseudoline notes (cote 154) are unpublished

ideas.what: Coning of cells from interior and boundary points, plus orange neighbourhood curves: a subdivision/star structure on the arrangement complex.
ideas.modern_name: Barycentric/stellar subdivision; regular neighbourhoods; links of strata
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses tame topology and stratified structures in general terms, not this construction

ideas.what: 'Unrolling' the neighbourhood of the boundary or line at infinity into a horizontal strip showing crossings (orange X) and oscillating cell profiles (green).
ideas.modern_name: Local picture near the line at infinity; related in spirit to wiring diagrams / allowable sequences
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goodman (1980) wiring diagrams; Goodman–Pollack allowable sequences

ideas.what: Row of triangles Δ/∇ on both sides of a line with abbreviated labels: apparently a case analysis of triangular cells adjacent to a line by side and orientation.
ideas.modern_name: Triangles adjacent to a pseudoline (Levi's lemma); triangle flips / Ringel moves
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926), Ringel (1956), Roudneff, Felsner et al.

missed.claim: The page documents Grothendieck working, in 1983-84, on the local cell structure of pseudoline arrangements near a line: dual graphs, boundary-adjacent cells, and triangles classified by side and orientation. This is independent of the contemporaneous Goodman–Pollack and oriented-matroid literature. The page itself contains no result beyond what is classical (Levi, Ringel), so it is mainly of historical interest.
missed.quote: p. a. h. / s.g.g. Δ ... ∇ ... i. g. a. i. out
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as documentation of the unpublished pseudoline project. The abbreviations might encode a classification scheme that could be compared with Ringel-move or triangle-flip combinatorics if decoded together with the surrounding pages.

deep.surprise_reason: These are exploratory sketches of an arrangement cell complex, its dual, and triangles adjacent to a line. All of it is standard combinatorial-geometry material, and no statements or new constructions are legible on this page.
transcription_corrections: The handwritten abbreviations are very uncertain; readings like 'p.d.h.' / 's.j.g.' are equally plausible. They sit next to the small Δ/∇ triangles (some hatched) drawn on a horizontal pencil baseline, which the transcription does not make clear.
Several of the left-hand labels are crossed out in the image, both lines of one pair (around 'p.a.h. / s.g.'), not only the one marked.

Several short dashed lines join the left disc drawing to the two wave diagrams. They are not mentioned in the transcription and indicate the wave diagrams are a developed view of the disc's boundary region.
The top-right pencil sketch includes small Λ-shaped triangles on the lower boundary of the circle and a hatched polygonal net in its upper right part.
The verso printout bulletin is from JESNEWS 1982 (C68 Cadarache), consistent with the next page, not generically 'CNUSC/CIRCE'.
